claims.claim: The business cycle is the economy's short-run movement from peak to trough and from trough back to peak — the recurring rise and fall of real economic activity.

The business cycle has four phases: expansion, a peak, contraction (recession), and a trough; the peak is the turning point from expansion to contraction and the trough is the turning point from contraction to expansion.
During an expansion, real GDP rises, businesses produce more, employment grows, and unemployment falls; a recession runs from peak to trough and an upswing from trough to peak.
A recession was historically defined as two consecutive quarters of declining GDP; this remains a common rule of thumb.

The NBER defines a recession as a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months, and it is the organization that tracks and officially dates U.S. business cycles.

The NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee applies three criteria — depth, diffusion, and duration — that are somewhat interchangeable, and it weighs a range of monthly measures, prioritizing real personal income less transfers and nonfarm payroll employment; it dates turning points retrospectively once enough data are available.
For the 2020 downturn the committee judged that the decline was so great and so widely diffused across the economy that it counted as a recession even though it proved very brief.

The NBER dates the 2007-2009 Great Recession from a peak in December 2007 to a trough in June 2009 (an 18-month contraction), and the 2020 COVID recession from a peak in February 2020 to a trough in April 2020 (a 2-month contraction, the shortest on NBER record).

Leading indicators tend to turn before the overall economy; the Conference Board's Leading Economic Index anticipates turning points by roughly seven months and includes components such as building permits, average weekly initial unemployment claims, the S&P 500, the interest-rate spread, and consumer expectations. Coincident indicators (payroll employment, personal income less transfers, industrial production, manufacturing and trade sales) move with real GDP, while lagging indicators such as the average duration of unemployment turn after the economy.

Real GDP follows a generally upward long-run path that short-term declines regularly interrupt; the business cycle is the short-run fluctuation around that long-run growth trend, which is a distinct phenomenon.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What officially counts as a recession in the United States
positions: Popular rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP
NBER official definition: a significant, broad decline in activity lasting more than a few months, judged by depth, diffusion, and duration across many monthly indicators
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the two-quarter rule as a widely used shortcut and the NBER definition as the official U.S. standard, naming the NBER as the arbiter and explaining that the two can diverge because the NBER does not mechanically count quarters.

sourceRecords.title: US Leading Indicators (Leading, Coincident, and Lagging Economic Indexes)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19 (component lists cross-checked against the Conference Board's Description of Components page in search results). Supports: the Leading Economic Index as a predictive tool that anticipates turning points in the business cycle by around seven months, with components including average weekly manufacturing hours, average weekly initial unemployment claims, manufacturers' new orders, the ISM new-orders index, building permits, the S&P 500, a leading credit index, the interest-rate spread (10-year Treasury minus the federal funds rate), and average consumer expectations; the Coincident Economic Index as reflecting current conditions and highly correlated with real GDP (payroll employment, personal income less transfers, manufacturing and trade sales, industrial production); and the existence of lagging indicators such as the average duration of unemployment and the unemployment rate that turn after the overall economy. Proprietary; no reuse license; REFERENCE_ONLY, used for the indicator framework only, in original prose.
